evidence.primary_claim: Sudō narrates parental abandonment, his father's janitorial work, and his pursuit of basketball; a prior sports-school recommendation was withdrawn following trouble. This is his retrospective self-account, not a verified independent family dossier.

Suzune presents a zodiac-position/surname-order explanation for VIP selection, illustrated by Rabbit/Karuizawa and Dragon/Kushida. It is the group's post-exam inference, not a newly published teacher-certified allocation formula.
Hirata proposes bringing Kushida into the Class D cooperation group; Suzune declines, claiming Hirata and Karuizawa provide needed interpersonal coverage.
School divides all three years into Red classes A/D and White classes B/C, with class-level and team-level consequences: losing team -100; grade-class positions +50,0,-50,-100.

Individual places score 15/12/10/8 for first-fourth and negative values from fifth; recommended events have 50/30/15/10 and doubled negative deduction from fifth; final relay triples recommended event values.

Top three individual event finishes permit a choice of 5000/3000/1000 private points or 3/2/1 written-test points; last place loses 1000 private points or a test point; bottom ten in each grade face -10 on the next written exam.

Festival has 13 published events; participation order is class-submitted before 17:00 the preceding day, no later edit, random assignment if missed, and eligible recommended-participant substitution costs 100000 private points per event.
Sudō volunteers for all recommended events, while Suzune warns repeated participation exhausts stamina; personal rewards compete with selecting the best participants for Class D.
Katsuragi and Hirata agree to minimize mutual interference as allied Red classes; Ryūen publicly refuses overt cooperation with Ichinose's White class, leaving intent uncertain.
Ayanokōji observes Class A gathering predominantly near Sakayanagi, suggesting a factional shift versus Katsuragi; the narrator's guess about motivations is not proof.

Ayanokōji distinguishes preparation (scouting and secrecy of order) from opportunistic rule manipulation, urges contingency planning against Ryūen and warns that his refusal to coordinate may be strategic.
Hirata articulates volunteer-choice versus ability-based assignment methods; Sudō supports emphasizing athletic competence while others prioritize chances at prizes.
Suzune proposes strength-based groupings and sharing earned private points; Shinohara and Karuizawa object to sacrificing non-athletes' personal rewards, and Kushida advocates a compromise.
Class D settles strategic disagreement through a show-of-hands vote, documenting conflicting collective and individual goals; do not infer the entire class unanimously agreed.

In grip-strength screening Ayanokōji deliberately stops at 60.6 rather than full effort, placing second behind Sudō with Kōenji uncounted; Hirata records 57.9, Ike 42.6 and Sotomura 42. These are observed readings, not absolute strength ceilings.

Hirata initially assigns tug-of-war using observed grip results, fills the scavenger-hunt field by a selection process involving chance, and warns classmates against photographing the provisional lineup.
Class C conspicuously does not scout Class D's public practices, which Ayanokōji treats as reason to suspect an already arranged plan; its existence is a hypothesis at this moment.
Sudō seeks permission to address Suzune by her given name if he wins first-year MVP, with a stated negative consequence if he fails; his personal motivation is explicitly involved.
Sudō demonstrates rope-pulling technique and coaches classmates intensely but impatiently; Hirata teaches carriage formations cooperatively and gently, contrasting leadership styles.
Horikita notices Ayanokōji's consistently average public athletics and asks whether he is hiding his ability; he denies it. Her suspicion is not first-person knowledge of his maximum.
Horikita and Onodera struggle to synchronize in three-legged practice, finishing third and quarreling; Hirata and Ayanokōji coordinate smoothly at practice speed; Sakura/Inogashira perform poorly.
Repeated failed pairings expose Suzune's refusal to accommodate a partner's pace; Ayanokōji offers practical feedback, while Kushida's popularity is considered an alternative for social coordination.
Ayanokōji proposes a Saturday recon meeting with Suzune and Kushida; he values Kushida's familiarity with other classes while withholding suspicions and private knowledge.
At a mixed-year soccer game, Hirata competes and interacts with Nagumo and Shibata; single plays do not supply quantitative career-level superiority.
Suzune confronts Kushida's hostility and her presence from prior junior high; Kushida maintains a public cooperative pose in front of others, while Kiyotaka remains cautious about her reliability.
Class D finalizes the lineup; Sudō's starting position reflects use of his explosive opening speed, while Suzune's preferred relay arrangement anticipates Manabu as anchor.
Sudō wins his 100-meter heat; Sotomura/Professor finishes last in the same heat; Kanzaki wins a different heat with Katsuragi third; Kōenji does not start his assigned heat.
Kōenji claims illness and withdraws; Sudō reacts aggressively and Hirata and Ayanokōji intervene. The narrator suspects malingering but no clinical diagnosis establishes it.
Sakura says she is not last in a 100-meter run for the first time; narrator frames this as improvement through effort, not proof of competitive speed.

Suzune narrowly beats Ibuki in their 100-meter heat; Ibuki starts quicker but repeatedly checks on Suzune. Kiyotaka attributes the loss partly to overattention, an interpretation not a measured speed difference.
Hirata acknowledges Shibata is faster than him in ordinary running; Manabu wins his observed third-year 100-meter heat; team running totals are announced 2011 Red versus 1891 White.
Ayanokōji places fifth in the 100 meters and third in hurdles while modulating effort; Kanzaki questions his apparent holding back. Yukimura reports seventh in two early races.
Suzune places third in hurdles behind Class C track athletes Yajima and Kinoshita; opposed runners being ahead in a hurdle race is not proof of globally superior athleticism.
In boys' capture-the-flag, Class C's forceful defense/attack and Ryūen's direct blow against Sudō contribute to the A/D defeat; the incident is portrayed as foul play, not an endorsed tactic.
Boys' tug-of-war exposes Red's internal Class A factional cooperation problem; Katsuragi intervenes to recover teamwork, while the B/C coalition changes formation and contests subsequent rounds.
Girls' ball toss proceeds in parallel with boys' events, but these pages do not supply an individually verified full placement matrix.

In obstacle race, Sudō defeats Shibata after rapid balance-beam traversal; Shibata closes during other obstacles. Ike finishes sixth in an earlier heat. Winner of this mixed-skill test is not necessarily fastest in a flat sprint.
Horikita and Kinoshita fall after contact in an obstacle race amid unusual matchups; who intentionally initiated contact remains uncertain from the immediate observation.

Three-legged race demonstrates teamwork demands: Hirata and Ayanokōji run together, while Horikita and Kushida coordinate under competitive pressure; specific universal ability rankings are not warranted.
In girls' cavalry battle multiple opponents target and overwhelm Suzune, who loses her headband; her isolated outcome is conditioned by four-on-one pressure.

Boys' cavalry battle shows Ryūen exploiting Hirata's attempted capture; Albert supports Ryūen and sustains strong contact; the D/A unit with Sudō loses, with allegations of a slippery headband unproven.
After repeated adverse matchups, Ayanokōji concludes Class D's participation table may have leaked to Ryūen; he cannot at that point prove the traitor's identity to the class.
Sudō explodes after taunting, rejects teamwork feedback and leaves the playing area; the loss removes a major athlete and aggravates team results.
Ryūen wins his observed 200-meter heat; Ayanokōji places third in his own 200-meter race; Sudō is absent for part of the event schedule.
Ayanokōji challenges Horikita to recognize both Sudō's emotional state and the probable compromised lineup; Horikita leaves at lunch to look for Sudō.
Ryūen and Kinoshita accuse Suzune of intentional foul play and invoke possible school penalties; Suzune maintains she did not deliberately injure anyone and seeks evidence.
Ryūen demands a private-point settlement in exchange for dropping the allegation; Suzune weighs severe exposure and refuses to treat a contested accusation as verified guilt.
After the accusation Suzune recognizes isolation and shortcomings in class strategy, then decides that reconnecting with Sudō is essential.

During the scavenger hunt Ayanokōji receives a difficult requirement involving bringing several friends; Ike performs well in his heat. The local event result cannot be turned into global social ability.
Suzune finds Sudō in the dorm and acknowledges his skill while confronting his temper and her own failure to lead; their conversation does not imply permanent behavioral reform.
Class D loses four-way tug-of-war with Sudō absent despite substitution; Kushida offers to join mixed three-legged event as a paid substitute after another participant withdraws.
In the mixed three-legged event Ayanokōji questions Kushida's knowledge of Class D's selection order and elicits defensive reactions; his suspicion is not yet public school-certified proof.
Kushida privately says she aims to expel Suzune and now adds Kiyotaka as a target; this is a character's declared future intent, not an already completed expulsion.
Suzune revisits Sudō before the relay, acknowledges the need for mutual support rather than solitary excellence, and persuades him to rejoin; he agrees on that occasion.
Ayanokōji replaces Miyake in relay under the paid-substitution rule after the latter reports an ankle issue; the dialogue suggests covert prior coordination with Hirata.
Sudō builds about fifteen meters of relay advantage as opener and Hirata maintains early momentum; subsequent legs lose ground, so this is not evidence of overall D superiority.

Ayanokōji and Manabu demonstrate extraordinary relay running; Manabu delays departure for their encounter, and Ayanokōji's path is obstructed by a falling runner. A clean straight-line comparison is unobserved.
During the relay Nagumo challenges Manabu's student-council philosophy and advances a stronger meritocratic agenda; political disagreement is separate from athletic ranking.
Red Team wins overall, but first-year class order B>C>A>D; net class points B 0, C -100, A -50, D -100. Shibata earns first-year MVP; Sudō does not.
Sudō pledges to control unjustified violence while Suzune recognizes she did not fulfill expectations; she permits him to use her given name despite his failure to win MVP.
Suzune openly confronts Kushida about their shared junior high and suspected betrayal in Ryūen's presence; Kushida acknowledges wanting students who know her past to disappear.

Kushida threatens to involve Manabu if Suzune exposes her past and vows to get Suzune expelled; Ryūen and Kushida discuss their cooperation. Threats are character claims and attempts, not school outcomes.

Ryūen describes using Kushida's leaked participant roster to engineer matchups and alleges Kinoshita rehearsed collision and accepted payment for a manufactured injury; narration does not establish a completed independent forensic investigation.
Suzune records Ryūen's account, but he counters with a longer video and characterizes his statements as hypothetical, defeating her unilateral editing threat.

An anonymous recording reaches Ryūen containing a previous strategy discussion featuring Ibuki; Ryūen concludes he faces a hidden counter-operator. The recording's contents and the Kinoshita narrative should not be flattened into identical witnessed events.
Suzune suspects Kiyotaka orchestrated the anonymous evidence and counterplay, but she lacks direct knowledge of its acquisition method or sender's confirmed identity.
Sakayanagi recognizes Kiyotaka, names the White Room and claims to have known him before he could remember her; he is unsettled and she frames their relationship as competitive.

Sakayanagi says she intends to defeat her father's greatest masterpiece and keep Kiyotaka's secret for now; Kiyotaka privately contemplates what his defeat would mean. Her knowledge source remains unproven here.

notes: One initial extraction pass is not a 104-item individually signed semantic review.
